power.name: Cross-language film remakes, built from the local film table alone
power.one_line: 105 documented remake pairs (80 listed) in which a story crosses a language border, so names and wording change; both plots of every pair are already in the local table, and the candidate pool is 92 documented sources plus 2,977 background plots whose unit presence is already computed.
power.lineage_definition: A lineage is a source film and the film or films that remake it in another language or film industry (Telugu to Tamil or Hindi, Malayalam to Hindi, Japanese or Hong Kong to American, American to Hindi, Korean to Chinese). A pair counts as documented when the lead of the remake's English Wikipedia article names the source as the film it remakes (or officially adapts). The documented source is the direct parent the lead names: Chandramukhi's is Apthamitra, not Apthamitra's own source. Left out: dubbed versions, films shot at once in two languages (they share one article and one plot), sequels, and same-language remakes (kept only as an optional contrast arm). Also left out of the primary set, by a rule to fix in advance: pairs where the remake's Wikipedia plot was copied from the source's article (10% or more of the remake's 5-word sequences found in the source). Those become the positive control.

power.expected_word_overlap:
Measured on the local table (first 40 sentences, sublinear TF-IDF; my own quick comparator, not the study's seven measures), on 103 of the 105 firm pairs.

- **Wording is independent.** The median TF-IDF cosine between a remake and its source is 0.19. The median share of the remake's 5-word sequences found in the source is 0.00.
- **Words still find most sources.** Among the other documented sources (about 60 eligible per remake), TF-IDF ranks the true source first for 82% of remakes on the texts as they are, and for 85% after a crude removal of capitalised words. For comparison, Batman's figure was 6 of 9 among 12 comics.
- **A pool of about 3,000 lowers that.** With the 2,977 background plots added as candidates, the source is first for 56% (texts as they are) and 74% (capitalised words removed). Words miss first place for 44 and 27 of the 103 remakes respectively, which is three to five times Batman's whole set.
- **Copying is common and has to be screened out.** Of 181 pairs with both plots long enough, 54 had the remake's plot copied from the source's article with names swapped. In all 54, words rank the source first.
- **Loose adaptations are where words fail.** In 24 Hollywood-to-Bollywood pairs that Wikipedia describes as "inspired by" or "unofficial remake", TF-IDF ranks the source first for 33% among documented sources and 12% to 33% among 3,000 candidates. Their documentation is softer, so they are not in the list of 80.

So this corpus does not remove the word ceiling. It gives the power to see whether units add anything under it.
power.names_differ_between_source_and_adaptati:
Yes, by the nature of the adaptation, and I measured it. In the 103 firm pairs the median share of the remake's capitalised words that also occur in the source is 7% (9% in the Indian pairs, 3% in the East Asian and Hollywood pairs). English same-language remakes share 20%.

What is still shared is mostly place names, common words that happen to be capitalised, and actors' names in brackets after a character's name. Those brackets must be stripped, because remakes often reuse an actor.

A few remakes keep character names: The Grudge shares 32% with Ju-On, the Telugu Gemini 36%, Drushyam 30%.

The practical gain is that the original texts become a clean condition for heredity. Names cannot carry the trail, so the test no longer depends only on the placeholder version. On the texts as they are, TF-IDF does slightly worse than with names removed (82% against 85% first), which confirms that names are noise here and not signal.
power.memorisation_risk:
Not checked: it needs the models. My expectation, by stratum:

- **East Asian and Hollywood pairs (about 19): high.** Seven Samurai, The Departed and The Ring are as famous as the 69 films Llama 3.3 70B named every time.
- **Indian pairs (about 86): probably lower, but unknown.** These are regional films from 1955 to 2017, and their English Wikipedia plots were still in the training data. Hits such as 3 Idiots or Ghajini will be recognised.

There is a second risk the Batman corpus also had: a model may know the remake relation itself, since the article's lead states it.

The paper's control transfers and gains power. Run the recognition probe on every name-free text, then compare how well units place the source for pairs where the model names both films against pairs where it names neither. With 105 pairs that split can show something; with 9 it could not.

This corpus does not solve memorisation. Only stories written after training do.
power.available_in_local_table:
Every plot the proposal needs is in the table.

- **The 105 firm pairs: 197 films, 92 distinct sources.** Both plots have at least 10 sentences. For the 80 listed, both have at least 15. Match by the Wiki Page column, not by Title: some rows have a cast list or a number as the title, some origins are wrong (the Tamil film Pizza is labelled Malayalam), and there are duplicate rows.
- **How the 105 were reached.** 198 pairs from my memory resolved to two rows of the table. 181 had both plots long enough. 54 of those were copied text. That left 103 firm and 24 loose pairs, and two more firm pairs were added by hand (Okkadu to Ghilli, Thuppakki to Holiday).
- **Decoy candidates cost no GPU.** The 2,977 background plots already have unit presence stored for all four models (`v2/acts/<model>/bg_present30.bits.npy`). About 520 are Indian films.
- **An optional same-language arm is also local.** Of 158 English-language remakes I listed from memory, 128 have both plots in the table with at least 10 sentences.

power.must_come_from_the_dump:
No plot text. Only the documentation:

- **The lead of each remake's article** (its first 1,000 characters or so), to quote the sentence that names the source. That is about 105 articles, found in one streaming pass over the shards.
- **Title changes since 2018.** The table's slugs are from about 2018 and some articles have moved (for example Bodyguard_(2009_film), Kick_(2014_Film), Son_Of_Sardaar). The plain-text dump has no redirects, so matching needs title variants plus year and language.
- **Optional expansion.** A search of all film leads for "remake of" would give a mechanical list. In the local 0.4% sample of the dump, about 20 of 1,190 film articles say so, most of them Indian cross-language remakes. That suggests a few thousand such articles overall, but only pairs with both plots in the 2017 table come free.
power.build_steps:
1. **Freeze the pair list from documentation only.** Start from the 105 firm pairs, confirm each lead in the dump and record the quoted sentence. Never select pairs by text similarity: that would bias the word baseline.
2. **Take the plots from the local table.** Join by Wiki Page slug, cut to 40 sentences with the study's own splitter (`fetch_corpus.sentences`), and require at least 12 sentences on both sides.
3. **Apply the copy screen, fixed in advance.** A pair goes to the positive-control set if 10% or more of the remake's 5-word sequences occur in the source. Here that is 54 pairs.
4. **Clean the texts.** Strip actors' names in brackets. Make name-free versions as in version 2, but treat the original texts as a first-class condition, since names differ naturally.
5. **Build the candidate pool.** Use all documented sources released before the remake, plus the background plots released before it. Define a near-neighbour pool by industry and decade.
6. **Remove overlap with the reference corpus.** 48 of the 356 films I looked up are among the 3,000 background plots and 134 are among the other reference plots. Take them out of base rates and out of the decoy pool, as version 2 did for one film.
7. **Run the study pass.** About 200 new texts in two versions, per model. The 2,999 background plots took 20 minutes on Qwen3-32B, so this is minutes.
8. **Compute the word comparators.** The same seven word measures, fitted on the background.
9. **Run the tests.**
   - The heredity statistic, tested by Monte Carlo relabelling within industry and decade. The exact enumeration is impossible at this size.
   - The residual test.
   - The recognition probe.
   - The copied pairs as positive control.
   - Two planned contrasts: official against loose pairs, and Indian against East Asian and Hollywood pairs.
10. **Write the plan and freeze it before any model reads a text.**
power.biggest_risks:
1. **The documentation is from my memory.** Live Wikipedia is unreachable. All 8 of my claims that happened to be checkable against the local dump sample matched (Policegiri, Vasool Raja MBBS, Ramaiya Vastavaiya, Lesa Lesa, Shakti: The Power, Coolie No. 1, About Last Night, The Mechanic), but only one of the 80 listed pairs is among them. A lead may say "based on" or "inspired by" where I remember "remake".
2. **Words still find most sources.** They are first for 82% to 85% among documented sources. The ceiling problem is reduced by pool size and by the number of pairs, not removed.
3. **The pool is weaker per candidate than Batman's.** The alternatives are unrelated stories from the same industry and period, not works of one universe. The size of the pool and same-industry matching compensate only partly. Only 13 of the 92 sources have two or more remakes, so within-family comparisons are few.
4. **Text quality is uneven.** The Indian plots are 2018 Wikipedia prose: uneven English, cast names in brackets, and a third of the pairs copied. The copy screen is itself a text rule and must be fixed before any result.
5. **Memorisation is unmeasured.** A model may also know the remake relation directly.
6. **The table has errors.** Wrong origin labels, titles replaced by cast lists, duplicate rows and a few wrong links.
7. **Identity and selection do not transfer** in the paper's sense.
8. **My numbers are rough.** The word baselines use my own quick TF-IDF and a crude removal of capitalised words. The power figure is a normal approximation.
power.what_each_outcome_would_show:
**What the size buys.** With 105 adaptations instead of 9, the smallest effect the rank test detects with 80% power falls from about 1 standard deviation of cell noise to about 0.25. That is my approximation, treating each adaptation's rank as uniform under the null.

- **Units find the sources and the residual test passes.** This would be the first evidence that neurons carry ancestry beyond word counts. It must then survive three checks: it holds on the original texts (so not the placeholders), it holds for pairs the model does not recognise (so not recall), and it holds in the Indian pairs alone.
- **Units find the sources and the residual test fails.** The paper's "absence of evidence" becomes a bounded negative: on Wikipedia plot summaries, units add nothing above about a quarter of a standard deviation to what words carry, even where names and wording changed.
- **Units do better only where words fail.** If units place the source well in the 27 to 44 remakes that words miss, or in the loose pairs, that points to story structure beyond vocabulary. It is the result most worth following up with rewritten stories.
- **Units fail to find sources that words find.** Then the strong-activation presence rule loses story signal that words keep, in line with the ablation hint in Section 4.2.
- **The positive control fails.** If units or words miss the copied pairs, the pipeline is broken.
power.which_experiments_it_supports:
- **Heredity: yes, and it is the purpose.** The same statistic, with 105 adaptations and a pool of 92 to about 3,000 candidates, against 9 and 12. The residual test gets real power, and the original texts become a usable condition.
- **Identity: only in a changed form.** There is no single lineage with a canon; families have 2 to 5 members. What can be asked is pairwise: do two tellings of one story share units more than a telling and a matched film from the same industry and decade? That is close to heredity, not a separate test of what makes a work recognisably itself.
- **Selection: not as designed.** Nothing here links a work's popularity to the spread of its units. A retention analysis is possible instead: which of a source's units survive into its remake, and whether the same units survive in independent remakes of one source. Only 13 sources have two or more remakes, so that is weak.

A franchise or one author's universe is still needed for identity and selection.
power.near_neighbour_negatives:
Plentiful for the pairwise question.

- The 2,977 background plots already have unit presence stored. About 520 are Indian (191 Hindi, 174 Tamil, 87 Telugu, 69 Malayalam), 107 are Japanese and 56 are Hong Kong films.
- The other 91 documented sources are popular commercial films of the same industries and decades.
- The table holds 4,521 Indian plots of 200 words or more, if closer matches by year, genre or director are wanted.

They are near neighbours by industry, period and genre, not by fictional universe. That is weaker than Batman's eight hero films in kind, and far stronger in number.
power.other_works:
- **Positive control: the 54 copied pairs.** For example Sethu with Seshu and Huchha, Chinna Thambi with Chanti, Thani Oruvan with Dhruva. Words rank the source first in all 54.
- **A loose stratum of 24 pairs, with softer documentation.** These are Hollywood-to-Bollywood adaptations whose articles say "inspired by" or "unofficial remake". Examples: Kaante from Reservoir Dogs, Heyy Babyy from Three Men and a Baby, Akele Hum Akele Tum from Kramer vs. Kramer, Mann from An Affair to Remember, Raaz from What Lies Beneath, Murder from Unfaithful, Humraaz from A Perfect Murder, Karz from The Reincarnation of Peter Proud, Malamaal Weekly from Waking Ned, Maryada Ramanna from Our Hospitality. Words rank the source first for only a third of them, so this is where units have most room.
- **An optional same-language arm of 128 English remakes.** Psycho, Cape Fear, The Fly, True Grit and the like. Names are shared (TF-IDF on the texts as they are puts the source first 97% of the time) and every film is famous. It would serve as a contrast, not as the primary set.
- **Chains for a parent-against-grandparent test.** Don to Billa (1980) to Billa (2007) to Billa (2009); Seven Samurai to The Magnificent Seven (1960) to its 2016 remake; Dial M for Murder to A Perfect Murder to Humraaz.
- **25 firm pairs not listed** because one plot has fewer than 15 sentences, such as The Outrage from Rashomon and Ek Ruka Hua Faisla from 12 Angry Men.
power.alternatives_rejected:
I could not measure any of these offline, because the books' and plays' plots are not local. The counts are from memory.

- **Stephen King.** About 55 film and miniseries adaptations, the firmest documentation of any option, and a truly near-neighbour pool of about 110 King works. Rejected as the primary because it has half the pairs, the source plots must come from the dump, names and wording are shared as in Batman, and it is heavily memorised. It is the best choice if identity and selection matter as much as heredity.
- **Agatha Christie.** A pool of 66 novels, but perhaps 35 to 45 adaptations with a usable plot section. Many television films have thin ones, and I am unsure of the count.
- **Shakespeare.** A pool of 37 plays and about 60 films including loose ones such as Ran and West Side Story. Straight adaptations often have no plot section of their own, and everything is maximally famous.
- **Sherlock Holmes, James Bond, Philip K. Dick, Roald Dahl.** Fewer than 30 pairs each with plots on both sides.
- **Jane Austen.** Only six candidate sources.
- **English same-language remakes as the primary.** 128 pairs are available locally, but names are shared and every film is famous. Kept as an optional arm.

replication.name: Sherlock Holmes: Conan Doyle's 60 stories and the screen works that draw on them (1929 to 2017)
replication.one_line: Swap Batman's 12 comics and 9 adaptations for the 60 Holmes stories and 33 screen works whose own Wikipedia articles name the story they draw on. I checked every title and plot section against live Wikipedia, which was reachable from this machine after all.
replication.lineage_definition:
A work is in the lineage if Sherlock Holmes is its detective.

The premise that live Wikipedia is unreachable was wrong in this session. The API and the pageviews API both answered through the proxy, slowly (6 to 30 seconds a request). I made about 280 small requests and cached them in my scratch folder. Everything marked "checked" below was read from the live articles on 8 November 2026. The November 2023 dump was not opened.

The lineage has four parts, mapped onto the Batman design:

1. **Candidate sources (Batman's 12 comics): 61.** The 60 canonical stories (4 novels and 56 short stories, 1887 to 1927) plus the pastiche novel The Seven-Per-Cent Solution (1974). All 60 canonical articles exist under the titles I give and each has a Plot section of 11 to 63 sentences (median about 29). Only one is under 12.
2. **Adaptations (Batman's 9): 33.** Each has a plot section of at least 8 sentences (the Batman fetcher's floor), and its own article names the source. They fall into three tiers by the article's wording:
   - A, straight adaptation: 7 (five Hound films, The Speckled Band 1931, The Sign of Four 1932).
   - B, "based on", "credited as" or "loosely based on": 12, plus the one pastiche pair.
   - C, "inspired by" or "incorporates elements of": 13.
   
   Together they make 45 adaptation-to-source links over 19 distinct canonical sources.
3. **Holmes works that adapt no story (Batman's 11 non-adapting screen works): 23** with usable plots. These are the baseline for the z-score and the later works for the selection test.
4. **Controls.** One title-only film, A Study in Scarlet (1933), whose article says the screenplay was original. Three films from Gillette's play, which has no plot section, are kept as lineage works only.

All 60 stories predate the earliest adaptation, so every story is an eligible candidate for every adaptation. The era-restricted relabelling Batman needed is not needed here.

I list 33 because that is what survived checking. From memory I had about 55 adaptations. Of 72 adaptation articles I probed, 33 are usable. The rest have no plot section, a plot of 1 to 6 sentences, or no article. Three titles (The Master Blackmailer, The Last Vampyre, The Eligible Bachelor) redirect to the story's own article, which would have created three fake perfect pairs.

replication.expected_word_overlap:
I measured this crudely on the live plot sections (first 40 sentences). Names were removed by dropping every word that appears capitalised away from a sentence start. Each adaptation was ranked against all 60 stories by plain TF-IDF cosine, with word weights from 4,000 plots of the local table.

**Result for the 32 adaptations with a canonical source (first-named source):**

- Ranked first of 60: 16 (50%).
- In the top three: 19.
- Below tenth place: 11 (34%).
- On average 16.5% of the other 59 stories beat the source, against 50% by chance.

| Tier | Adaptations | Source ranked first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A, straight adaptation | 7 | 7 |
| B, credited or loosely based | 12 | 6 |
| C, elements | 13 | 3 |

The pairs plain words miss are the loose ones: A Scandal in Belgravia (19th), The Empty Hearse (45th), Sherlock Holmes Faces Death (27th), Zero Effect (39th), The Woman in Green (26th), Dressed to Kill (29th), Terror by Night (23rd).

**What to expect.** Words will again pass the heredity test overall, about as strongly as on Batman (11% against 46% by chance, the source first for 6 of 9). The difference is that a third of the pairs are not found by plain words. Batman had no such stratum. Those pairs are where units could add something, or where the summaries carry no trace at all.

For comparison, the same crude method on James Bond (26 films from the local table against the 14 Fleming books) ranks the source first for 12 of 18 pairs, the same two-thirds as Batman.

**Limits of this check.** The name removal is cruder than the study's rewriter. It uses one word measure, not the study's seven. It is not the study's z-scored statistic. Ranks moved by one place between two runs with different vocabularies.
replication.memorisation_risk:
High, and I did not measure it; no model was run.

- The stories are out of copyright and among the most reproduced texts in English, and the Sherlock episodes are heavily summarised online. Expect the 70B model to name the story for nearly every name-free source and most adaptations, as it named Batman for 29 of 32 works.
- The live text of November 2026 postdates every model's training, but the stories behind it do not. No work in this corpus postdates the models.
- A second franchise cannot fix this. What it adds is enough pairs to split the heredity test by whether the model names the source. That needs both kinds to exist, which is itself uncertain.
- The less famous works are the likeliest not to be named: the nine Universal films of 1942 to 1946, the two German Hound films (1929, 1937), Zero Effect and the 2014 game.
- If recognition drives the result, the title-only control (A Study in Scarlet, 1933) should behave like a non-adaptation.
replication.names_differ_between_source_and_adaptati:
Mostly no, so the placeholder problem is repeated here and not fixed.

- Holmes, Watson, Moriarty and Lestrade keep their names in every pair but one.
- Case-specific names often change. The Universal films use new characters. Sherlock renames some (Milverton becomes Magnussen, Sir Henry Baskerville becomes Henry Knight).
- Zero Effect changes every name. It is the one pair that could be run with no name removal.

A like-for-like run would replace names with codes exactly as before, with the same caveat about the mark the codes leave.

replication.which_experiments_it_supports:
All three, plus the recognition probe.

- **Identity.** 56 Holmes screen works and 61 sources against 162 detective films, where Batman had 8 negatives.
- **Heredity and the residual test.** 33 adaptations against 61 candidate sources, where Batman had 9 against 12. Each rank is out of 60, not about 8, so each pair says more. The three tiers allow a pre-registered split into straight, credited and elements.
- **Selection.** 60 early works with a 52-fold spread of pageviews, spreading into 23 later works that adapt nothing. By the same calculation that gives the paper's 27% for 15 works, 60 works give about 75% power against a true correlation of 0.3.
- **Positive control in place of Batman's 7 sequels.** At least five sequel pairs exist: A Game of Shadows after Sherlock Holmes (2009), Enola Holmes 2 after Enola Holmes, The Empty Hearse after The Reichenbach Fall, A Scandal in Belgravia after The Great Game, and The Final Problem (Sherlock) after The Lying Detective. The five Hound films should also find each other.

It does not by itself support steering or ablation. The ablation could be repeated on a Holmes canon at small cost.

replication.build_steps:
1. **Freeze the lists first.** Write the work list, the pair list with its three tiers, and the analysis plan, and commit them before any model reads a Holmes text, as `PLAN.md` was. Decide then:
   - the primary set (I suggest tiers A and B with the first-named source, and tier C as a registered secondary);
   - how to treat the six works on The Hound (average within a source, or cap at three);
   - the positive control.
2. **Fetch the plot sections** with the logic of `study/fetch_corpus.py` (first 40 sentences, floor of 8). Record the resolved title of every page and reject any adaptation whose title resolves to its source's article.
3. **Remove names** with the existing protocol (`study/make_neutral.py`) for about 290 new texts: 121 lineage works, 162 negatives and 5 ancestors.
4. **Build the negatives** from the local table by the rule above, matched to the Holmes screen works by decade and length.
5. **Handle the reference overlap.** Run `study/v2/check_reference_overlap.py` on the new list. Drop the three Holmes films from the background plots, or show that 3 in 2,999 does not move a base rate.
6. **Fetch pageviews** with `study/fetch_extras.py` for the selection test.
7. **Run the four models.** Scales and base rates already exist.
8. **Generalise the experiment code.** The `ADAPTATIONS`, `SCREEN_NONADAPT` and `SEQUELS` tables in `study/experiments.py` become data files. Relabelling 61 sources cannot be enumerated, so it becomes a Monte Carlo permutation.
9. **Run the recognition probe** on every text and report heredity separately for works the model does and does not name.

My checks are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-phylomemetics/a789a30b-498f-5fe1-bc57-f1de263eb0f6/scratchpad/corpus/franchise/`:

replication.biggest_risks:
1. **Words may still win.** Plain words already rank the source first for half the pairs. The gain over Batman is power and a stratum words miss, not a corpus where words fail.
2. **Recognition.** These are the best-known detective stories there are. A pass on heredity or identity in the 70B model would carry the same doubt as on Batman.
3. **Fewer independent sources than pairs.** The 33 adaptations rest on 19 distinct sources, and 6 are The Hound. Thirteen are episodes of one series, written by the same people and probably summarised by the same editors. Effective sample size is nearer 20 than 33.
4. **Tier C is weakly documented.** The wording is "inspired by", "uses minor plot elements", "the title is inspired by". If neither words nor units find these, that says little about either.
5. **Uneven lengths.** Sources run from 12 to 63 sentences and adaptations from 13 to 49. The openings analysis is needed again.
6. **Placeholders again.** Names are the same in source and adaptation, so the codes and their mark return.
7. **Identity may again be names and period.** The Holmes works cluster in 1939 to 1946 and 2010 to 2017; unmatched negatives would turn it into a test of era.
8. **Coverage is thinner than memory suggests.** 39 of the 72 adaptation articles I probed were unusable. Almost every television film of The Hound and The Sign of Four from 1972 to 2002 has no plot section. Any proposal built from memory alone should be discounted by about half.
9. **Wikipedia moves.** Lengths are as of 8 November 2026 and the dump is three years older.

**What I could not check**

- No model was run.
- The dump was not opened.
- The pair counts I give for Spider-Man, X-Men, Superman, Star Trek, Godzilla and Doctor Who are from memory. Only Holmes and Bond were checked live.
- There may be Holmes adaptations with their own articles that I did not think to probe.

**One side effect to report.** Running the project's Python may have written two or three bytecode cache files inside the git-ignored `.venv`. Nothing tracked was touched, and the other files changed today under `study/v2` are not mine.
replication.what_each_outcome_would_show:
**Heredity supported, residual test still null.** With 33 pairs, 61 candidates and a third of the sources not found by plain words, the Batman null was not just low power. Under this presence rule the units add nothing to words even where words fail. That would be a much firmer negative, and it would point at the planted-story experiment.

**Heredity supported and the residual test passes, mainly in the pairs words miss.** This would be the first evidence that units carry ancestry that words do not. It would count only if it also holds among adaptations the model does not name, and if the title-only control stays at chance.

**Neither words nor units find the tier C pairs.** Then "inspired by" leaves no measurable trace in a plot summary. That is a limit of the corpus, and the claim should rest on tiers A and B.

**Identity passes against 162 detective films.** Batman's failure was then about superheroes and 8 negatives, not about name-free canons in general. Check it against period and against the model's recognition.

**Identity fails again.** The finding that a canon is names plus genre holds for a second franchise.

**Selection.** With 60 early works and about 75% power, a null would for the first time say something. A positive result would need controls for length and for how often a story is adapted.

**The 70B model names nearly every story.** Recognition then confounds a second franchise in the same way. Only rewritten or post-training stories can separate what units detect from what the model remembers.
replication.alternatives_rejected:
**James Bond, the runner-up (checked).**

- All 26 films to 2015 are in the local table with 23 to 40 sentences each (median 680 words).
- All 14 Fleming books have live plot sections of 18 to 43 sentences.
- It yields only about 18 film-to-book pairs with real content and 14 candidate sources.
- The crude word check ranks the source first for 12 of 18, the same two-thirds as Batman, so it would repeat Batman at twice the size.
- Its sequels share few plot words (Quantum of Solace ranks Casino Royale 24th of 25), so the positive control would be weak.
- Its strengths are the cleanest texts of any candidate and three built-in title-only controls (The Spy Who Loved Me, A View to a Kill, Quantum of Solace). It is the right third franchise.

**The others.** The table counts are checked; the pair counts are from memory.

- **Spider-Man.** 6 films in the table and about 8 to 10 adaptations of a named storyline. No gain over Batman's 9.
- **X-Men.** 11 films in the table and about 9 pairs (God Loves, Man Kills; The Dark Phoenix Saga; Days of Future Past; Old Man Logan). Same size as Batman.
- **Superman.** About 11 pairs, mostly animated films that follow their comic closely, so words would win. It shares a universe with Batman (Batman v Superman is already a study work), so it is not independent.
- **Star Trek.** 13 films in the table and hundreds of episode articles, but the links are sequels and callbacks (The Wrath of Khan to Space Seed), which are the positive control in this design, not the test.
- **Godzilla.** 34 films in the table but one medium. The documented links are re-edits and reboots of the 1954 film, with no pool of sources.
- **Doctor Who.** 2 films in the table and about 6 to 8 documented adaptations in all.

**Not asked for, but considered.**

- **Marvel pooled across characters.** It might reach 35 to 40 pairs, but it is a publisher and not one hero, so the identity test loses its meaning and most sources are "inspired by".
- **Agatha Christie.** Many pairs, but nearly all faithful, so words would find every source.

divergence.name: Transposed retellings: 80 renamed, relocated adaptations of 48 classic sources
divergence.one_line: Not one franchise but 48 small lineages: 80 screen retellings that rename the characters and move the story (Romeo and Juliet to West Side Story, Macbeth to Throne of Blood, Seven Samurai to The Magnificent Seven), each ranked against 72 candidate sources. A pilot on the local table shows word counts still find most sources here, so the gain is nine times the pairs, no placeholder codes, and a block where words are weak, not a corpus where words fail.
divergence.lineage_definition: A lineage is one source work (a play, novel, tale, epic or film) and the screen works that retell it under other names in another time, place or genre. A pair enters the confirmatory set when three things hold. (1) The adaptation's English Wikipedia article says, in its lead, infobox or production section, that it is based on, adapted from, a retelling of or a remake of the source. Tier A is a credit or a flat statement of adaptation. Tier B is 'loosely based on' or 'inspired by' on the makers' word. Tier C, where only critics make the link, is kept as a small contested block that every analysis is also run without. (2) The protagonists are renamed and the setting is moved; surviving secondary names (Elton, Darcy, Kurtz, Cassio) are recorded per pair, not edited. (3) Both works have a plot or synopsis section of about 200 words or more. For each adaptation the candidate sources are all 72 source texts older than it: 48 with at least one listed adaptation and 24 decoys that are close relatives of them (other Shakespeare plays, other Austen and Victorian novels, other fairy tales, other westerns and noirs). Two control strata sit beside the 80: faithful screen versions with the names kept (positive control, and a second independent Wikipedia description of the source), and partly renamed versions (She's the Man, Gnomeo and Juliet, Joe MacBeth).

divergence.expected_word_overlap:
I measured this, and the premise holds only in part. Using the paper's TF-IDF (same settings) on the 59 of the 80 pairs that can be computed from the local table alone, with each literary source stood in for by a faithful film of it, against a pool of 54 source texts:

- Faithful versions with the names kept (15 controls): mean cosine to the source 0.45, source ranked first for 14 of 15.
- The transposed pairs: mean cosine 0.11, a quarter of that. But the documented source is still ranked far above chance: 11.7% of wrong sources beat it (standard error 2.8 points; chance 50%), against 11% for TF-IDF on Batman. Against only the 11 sources most like the true one it is 15.9%.
- The source is ranked first for 28 of 59 (Batman: 6 of 9), worse than fifth for 20, worse than tenth for 11.
- With capitalised words removed the figures barely move (10.8%, first for 23 of 59), so it is plot vocabulary, not leaked names, that carries the trail.

By block: Shakespeare 17.3% (first for 5 of 19); novels and plays 9.1% (15 of 25); fairy tales 16.7% (3 of 6); film-to-film genre shifts 3.8% (5 of 9). A wider pilot of 109 transposed pairs against 84 sources gave the same picture: 9.6% overall, 5.2% for film sources, 13.4% for literary ones.

So words fail outright on about a fifth of pairs (Warm Bodies, Easy A, Ball of Fire, The Nutty Professor, All Night Long, The Lion King II, Romeo Must Die) and succeed on the rest. Two things were not checked: the real source synopses (plays and novels, from the dump) may overlap more or less than the film stand-ins, and 21 of the 80 pairs had no stand-in or no table entry.
divergence.memorisation_risk:
High, and of a new kind. These are famous works with their names left in, so recognition will be higher than on Batman's name-free texts (where Llama 3.3 70B already named every ordinary film). Worse, the models know the links themselves: that Clueless is Emma and West Side Story is Romeo and Juliet is common knowledge. A unit could fire for the source because the model recalls the fact, not because it reads the story's shape. That would pass a 'beyond words' test for the wrong reason.

What the design does about it:
- A link probe before any unit analysis: each model is asked, for each adaptation, which work it is and which older work it retells. Every result is reported separately for pairs where it names the link and pairs where it does not.
- An obscure block is built in: about 25 of the 80 are Indian films, 1940s to 1960s B pictures or little-known titles (Jubal, All Night Long, Men of Respect, The Badlanders, Man Pasand, Kandukondain Kandukondain, Dangerous Liaisons 2012). I expect the smaller models not to know these links, but have not tested it.
- A sensitivity version with the adaptation's names swapped for other ordinary names (not codes), which removes recognition by name and leaves no placeholder mark.
- Not solved here: a block of retellings released after the models' training (2024 to 2026) would be the only clean test. It is not in the November 2023 dump and live Wikipedia is not reachable from this machine.
divergence.names_differ_between_source_and_adaptati: Mostly, and without any edit. Of the 59 pairs I could check, 38 share no proper noun with the source text and do not name the source or its author (the true count is about 40; the crude check flags three character names such as Homer and Connell by mistake). The other 19 or so leak in two ways. Some keep a secondary name: Elton (Clueless), Darcy (Bridget Jones's Diary), Cassio (O), Merteuil (Cruel Intentions), Edward and Lucy (From Prada to Nada), Friday (Robinson Crusoe on Mars), Elsinore (Strange Brew), Kurtz (Apocalypse Now, not in the 59). Others have a plot text that names its source: Maqbool opens 'The film is based on William Shakespeare's Macbeth', and Omkara, Get Over It, Scrooged, Whatever It Takes, Trishna, Ever After and Easy A do something similar. The fix is to cut sentences that name the source or author (they are not plot), record the count of shared names per pair, add it to the word measures that are regressed out, and report the zero-shared-name subset on its own. No placeholder codes are needed anywhere.
divergence.near_neighbour_negatives:
For identity, each lineage's negatives are the retellings of every other source: about 70 to 75 per lineage against Batman's 8, and they include close relatives (retellings of other Shakespeare tragedies for Macbeth, of other courtship novels for Emma, of other fairy tales for Cinderella). Lineages large enough to test, counting the reserve list: Romeo and Juliet (6 to 9 retellings), Hamlet (5), Cinderella (4 to 5), Othello (4), Cyrano (3 to 5), The Most Dangerous Game (3 to 4), Macbeth (3 to 4), Seven Samurai (2 to 5).

A word-count pilot on the table (TF-IDF centroid of the other retellings, held-out member against about 100 other retellings) shows where there is room. Words are weak for Othello (AUC 0.60, 0.53 with names removed), Hamlet (0.64, 0.71), Romeo and Juliet (0.73, 0.77), Cyrano (0.76, 0.55) and Seven Samurai (0.77, 0.75). Words already solve Cinderella (1.00) and The Most Dangerous Game (0.95). These lineages have four to seven members each, so each AUC is rough.

divergence.build_steps:
1. Freeze the pair list and its tiers before any model reads a text. Check each 'unsure' entry against the article text in the dump (lead and production section) and move it to the contested block or drop it. Do not select or drop pairs by their word-overlap rank.
2. Pull the 74 adaptation plots, 9 film sources, 27 faithful witnesses and the partly renamed controls from the local table. Strip cast names in brackets and reference marks.
3. One scan of the dump for about 100 titles: 59 source synopses (39 with adaptations, 20 decoys), 7 adaptations, longer versions of short plots.
4. Cut every sentence that names the source, its author or its characters as such. Record what was cut and the count of shared proper nouns per pair.
5. Keep the first 40 sentences, and also build the length-matched openings the paper uses.
6. Run the link probe and the title probe on all four models, then the units.
7. Heredity: for each adaptation rank its documented source among all older sources; test by relabelling sources (Monte Carlo, since 72 sources are too many for an exact test), which keeps adaptations of one source together. Then the residual test with the paper's seven word measures plus the shared-name count.
8. Report all 80, then without the contested block, the zero-shared-name subset, the link-unknown subset, and each block (Shakespeare, novels, tales, films) on its own.
9. Run the same on the faithful and partly renamed controls: words and units must both find those.
divergence.biggest_risks:
1. Words still carry most of the trail. In the pilot TF-IDF does as well here as on Batman by the paper's own statistic (11.7% against 11%). The corpus does not remove the problem; it gives a test with enough pairs to see past it, and a Shakespeare block where words are weaker (17%).
2. Recall of the link. A pass could mean the model knows Clueless is Emma. Only the link-unknown subset is clean, and I cannot say how large it will be until the probe is run.
3. Documentation is uneven and partly from my memory. Seven entries are marked unsure and four are contested (The Bad Sleep Well, Jubal, Forbidden Planet, and Warm Bodies at film level). Live Wikipedia was not reachable, so none was verified.
4. Unequal texts. A play's act-by-act synopsis and a film plot are different registers; fairy-tale plots may be a fifth the length of a film's. Length must be controlled as the paper does.
5. Dependence. Six pairs share Romeo and Juliet, and 48 sources carry 80 pairs, so the effective sample is nearer 48 than 80. Relabelling sources handles this in the test but power is less than 80 suggests. As a rough guide, a 10-point residual effect is about 1 standard error with 9 pairs and 2 to 3 with these.
6. Selecting on words. Choosing pairs because TF-IDF fails on them would make units look better than words by regression to the mean. The list must be fixed by rule.
7. Multiple sources. Phantom of the Paradise, The Lion King and Ran each name more than one source.
8. The pilot used film stand-ins for literary sources; the real synopses may behave differently.
divergence.what_each_outcome_would_show:
- Units find the sources, and still do once the word measures are regressed out, in the link-unknown subset as well: neurons see a story's ancestry beyond its words. This is the result the Batman corpus could not give either way.
- The residual passes only where the model names the link: the units carry the model's knowledge of the adaptation, not a reading of the story. That is a finding about recall and should be reported as such.
- Units find the sources but nothing is left after the word measures: the same answer as Batman, now with about 80 pairs and names that differ naturally, so 'too few pairs' and 'placeholder marks' are no longer available as explanations. That would be a much firmer negative.
- Units fail where words succeed (film-to-film block) and also where words fail (Warm Bodies, Ball of Fire, Easy A): neurons are a worse tracer than word counts on plot summaries.
- Units beat words only on the Shakespeare block: a narrower claim, that units help where plot vocabulary has been replaced, worth a follow-up on that block alone.
- Identity: if a lineage's shared units tell Othello or Hamlet retellings from other retellings where words reach only 0.53 to 0.71, that is a name-free identity the Batman test could not show. If Cinderella passes and Othello fails, units are tracking vocabulary.
- If the faithful controls fail, the pipeline is broken and nothing else should be read.
divergence.which_experiments_it_supports: Heredity and the residual test: yes, this is what it is built for (80 pairs, 72 candidate sources, against 9 and 12). Identity: yes for five to eight lineages, each with about 70 near-neighbour negatives, though each lineage has only three to nine members. Selection: no. There is no usable measure of which early retellings were popular and no dated chain of descent long enough; the paper's own power problem would be worse here.
divergence.alternatives_rejected:
- Straight cross-cultural remakes (Ring to The Ring, Infernal Affairs to The Departed, Hollywood to Bollywood). The table holds dozens with both plots, so they need no dump. But the pilot shows words find them easily (5.2% of wrong sources beat the true one over 51 film-source pairs), so they repeat Batman's ceiling. Ten genre-shift cases are kept as the block where words should win.
- A single franchise of retellings (all Romeo and Juliet, or all Cinderella). One source gives no wrong-source pool, and Cinderella is already solved by words (AUC 1.00).
- Critics-only parallels (Disturbia and Rear Window, where a court found no copying; Pale Rider and Shane; A Bug's Life and Seven Samurai; Trading Places and The Prince and the Pauper). Words fail on several of these, which is tempting, but the lineage is opinion.
- Choosing only pairs where TF-IDF fails. It would manufacture a win for units.
- Redacting the leaked names with codes. It brings back the placeholder mark.

memorisation.lineage_definition:
A lineage is a remake family: one original film and the later films that English Wikipedia documents as remakes of it in a different Indian film industry. A documented pair is (remake, original), where the remake's article names the original as the film it remakes.

Rules, to be fixed before any model reads a text:
1. Both films are in the local table and each plot has at least 15 sentences by the repository's splitter (fetch_corpus.sentences).
2. The two films come from different industries among Hindi ("Bollywood" in the table), Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada.
3. Dubbed releases, films shot in two languages at once, sequels and "inspired by" cases are not pairs.
4. A pair is left out when the two summaries share 10% or more of their word 5-grams after names are stripped, because one Wikipedia summary was pasted from the other.
5. When a remake was itself remade, the source is the film the article names.

Candidate sources for each remake are the 70 originals in the set that are not later than it. A second, harder pool is every film of the source's industry in the table.

memorisation.build_steps:
About two days of work and a few dollars of GPU.

1. **Freeze the rules and the analysis plan** before any model reads a text.
2. **Clean the table** (half a day).
   - Keep one row per Wikipedia page and per plot text.
   - Drop bracketed actor names, footnote marks and sentences about the film itself ("This movie is a remake of ...").
   - Keep the first 40 sentences by fetch_corpus.sentences and require 15.
3. **Take the documentation from the dump** (one day, mostly the 20 GB download and the reading).
   - For every film page in the table, cut the lead and any "Remakes" section from wikimedia/wikipedia 20231101.en.
   - Match "remake of the <year> <language> film <title>" and "remade in <language> as <title>", and resolve titles by year and language.
   - A person reads every match (about 300 lines) and stores the quoted sentence with each pair.
   - Derive the final pair list from this, not from my list. My 78 are a check on recall.
4. **Compare each table plot with the dump's plot section** for the same page, to catch wrong-article rows.
5. **Apply the pasted-wording rule** (under 10% shared 5-grams on name-stripped text) and report the set without it too.
6. **Run recognition first.** Ask each model which film each plot summarises and which film it remakes.
7. **Run the GPU pass** on the 180 study texts and the 3,604-film pool, through the existing study pass and scales.
   - Rebuild the reference-only scale leaving out the study films that are in the reference corpus. finalize_scale.py takes a list of documents, and 24 strongest examples are stored per unit.
   - Take base rates from the 544 Indian films already among the 3,000 background plots, minus study films.
8. **Analyse.**
   - E2 on the 70 sources, with a Monte Carlo relabelling null (70 sources cannot be enumerated exactly).
   - The residual decision test with the seven word measures.
   - The rank of the source among all films of its industry, for units and for TF-IDF.
   - Split each by pasted or independent wording, by whether the model names the films, and for the East Asian block.
memorisation.biggest_risks:
1. **It does not fix the word-overlap limit.** A remake retells its source scene by scene, so word counts find these sources more easily than Batman's. On the 70-source pool the E2 statistic cannot separate units from words. Only the residual test and whole-industry retrieval can, and the second rests on 16 to 40 hard pairs.
2. **Recognition is unknown until the probe is run.** If Llama 3.3 70B names most of these films, the main reason for choosing this corpus goes.
3. **The pair list rests on my memory.** I am sure of 75 and fairly sure of three (Samrat, Bharathan, Khuddar). My list also leans towards films I remember, which are the better-known ones. The list should be rebuilt from the dump's leads.
4. **The table has errors.** One of the 14 lowest-similarity pairs I read held the wrong film's plot. I read the plot openings of the 50 lowest-similarity pairs, not all 78.
5. **The pasted-wording rule uses a word measure to choose pairs.** It must be fixed in advance and reported both ways.
6. **Overlap with the reference corpus.** 90 of the 147 films are in it and 27 are among the 3,000 background plots. Scales and base rates must leave them out.
7. **There is no single lineage.** The paper's identity test (a canon across 32 works) and selection test have no counterpart here.
8. **Text quality.** These are fan-written summaries, some in poor English.
9. **Limit (2) needs different material.** Loose adaptations, or the source put into another language, would address it. I did not scope either.

**Side effects of this scouting run.** I ran one read-only `git status` by mistake, against the rule. Importing networkx also wrote 286 bytecode cache files under .venv, which I left in place. Nothing else in the repository was touched.
memorisation.which_experiments_it_supports:
- **Heredity: yes, the main use.** 78 pairs against 9, across 70 unrelated lineages.
- **Residual test (do neurons add to words): yes, with far more power.** There are 78 x 69 = 5,382 non-source cells against 99. A second form, retrieval among all films of the industry, is one where words are not at ceiling.
- **Identity: only in a changed form.** There is no lineage of 32 works, so there is no canon. Two things can be tested:
  - whether a remake is closer to its own source than to its near neighbours, which is the heredity test with hard negatives;
  - on the 22 families of three to five films among the 154 verified pairs, whether units shared by the other members pick out the held-out member.
- **Selection: no.** The table has no popularity measure and the families are too small. The nearest question is whether the units one remake keeps are the units another remake of the same film keeps; 8 sources in the set have two remakes.
memorisation.what_each_outcome_would_show:
- **Units find the sources, including for films the model cannot name.** The Batman heredity result is not a product of shared names, placeholder codes or the model knowing the story.
- **Units find the sources only where the model names the films, and in the East Asian block.** The trail is recognition.
- **The residual test passes, and units rank the source well in the pairs where TF-IDF puts it worse than 10th among 3,600 films.** This would be the first evidence that neurons carry something word counts do not. Because the summaries were written independently and the names differ, it would be story content.
- **The residual test fails with 78 pairs.** That is a well-powered null: on retellings of the same plot, neurons under this presence rule add nothing to words. The Batman null was then not just a matter of 9 pairs, and only stories reworded on purpose (the planned planted-story experiment) remain.
- **Units do well only on the 65 pasted pairs.** Units follow wording.
- **Units fail to find sources that TF-IDF finds.** The strong-activation rule loses the story signal, and the Batman heredity result leaned on Batman's shared vocabulary.
memorisation.alternatives_rejected:
- **East Asian originals with American remakes as the main set.** Only 17 pairs have both plots in the table. Many originals are missing (Oldboy, My Sassy Girl, A Tale of Two Sisters, Il Mare), and only 107 of the 522 South Korean plots reach 15 sentences. These are also the films a model is most likely to recognise. Kept as the contrast block.
- **Hindi remakes of American or Korean films.** Mostly unofficial, so not documented, and the originals are the most memorised.
- **Same-industry remakes (Don, Agneepath, Zanjeer).** Only 11 pairs, all famous.
- **Using all 154 Indian pairs.** 42% have pasted summaries, where any measure wins trivially. Kept as a positive control.
- **Choosing pairs by plot similarity.** It finds about 96 more pairs but selects for high word overlap, so it was used only to count.
- **Another single franchise from the table (Godzilla, Kamen Rider, Doraemon).** No documented adaptation-source pairs, and they are recognisable.
- **Taking one side from Tamil, Telugu or Hindi Wikipedia.** This would remove word overlap altogether, but unit scales and base rates exist only for English text, and I could not check how many of those articles have plot sections.

scores.comment: Sherlock Holmes. The only franchise among the four, and the only one where identity, heredity and selection all run as designed. Heredity: 32 adaptations with a canonical source against 60 stories (Batman: 9 against 12), but the cleanly documented set (tiers A and B) is 19 adaptations on 12 sources, 6 of them on The Hound, and 13 of the 32 are episodes of one series. Identity: 56 screen works against about 160 detective films chosen by rule (Batman: 8). Selection: 60 early works, about 75% power where Batman had 27%. Words rank the source first for 16 of 32 and miss 11, but the missed ones are mostly the weakly documented 'elements' pairs. Names are kept, so the placeholder codes return. These are the best-known detective stories there are, so recognition will be at least as bad as for Batman. Feasibility is the strongest of the four: the scout fetched and cached 201 live articles, and I confirmed that live Wikipedia answers from this machine and that the film table holds what the scout says.

Cross-language remakes, 105 pairs, every plot already in the local table. The best-powered test of whether units add anything to words, and names differ by themselves, so the original texts can be used with no codes. But words find these sources more easily than Batman's (source first for 82% to 85% among documented sources, against 6 of 9), and the only stratum where words fail (24 'inspired by' Hollywood-to-Hindi pairs) has soft documentation. Recognition is unmeasured: probably low for regional Indian films, high for the 19 East Asian and Hollywood pairs. Documentation is from memory for 104 of 105 pairs; that can now be checked live in an hour or so, since Wikipedia is reachable. It is not a franchise: no canon, so no identity test in the paper's sense, and no selection test.

Transposed retellings, 80 pairs on 48 sources. The only proposal aimed at the word problem, and its own pilot shows it mostly does not solve it: words do as well as on Batman overall (11.7% against 11%), and fail outright on about a fifth of pairs. Recognition is the worst of the four, in a new way: names are left in, the works are famous, and the links themselves are common knowledge (Clueless is Emma), so a pass could be recall of a fact. The build is the heaviest: 59 source synopses and 7 films still to fetch, plays and fairy tales in a different register and length from film plots, sentences to cut by hand, 7 pairs unsure and 4 contested, and the pilot used film stand-ins for the literary sources. Identity is possible only for five to eight lineages of three to nine works. No selection.

Indian cross-industry remakes, 78 pairs, with 17 famous East Asian pairs as a contrast block. Essentially the same corpus as 'power' under stricter rules (15 sentences, pasted summaries screened out). Its design is the cleanest answer to recognition: a main set of mostly obscure regional films against a block the models should recognise, with the recognition question asked first. Still unmeasured, and names stay in the text. Words are at ceiling, as the scout says itself: the source is first for 62 of 78 and only 1.2% of other sources beat it, so the heredity statistic cannot separate units from words; only the residual test and retrieval among a whole industry can. Not a franchise: no identity or selection test.

first_author_aims.recommendation:
Sherlock Holmes (key: replication).

Why this one:

1. It is the only franchise among the four, which is what the request asks for, and the only proposal where all three experiments run as designed.
   - Identity: 56 Holmes screen works against about 160 detective films picked by rule (Batman: 32 against 8).
   - Heredity: 32 adaptations with a canonical source, each ranked among 60 stories (Batman: 9 among 12).
   - Selection: 60 early works with a 52-fold spread of pageviews, about 75% power against a true correlation of 0.3 (Batman: 27%). I checked that figure and it is right.
   The other three proposals drop identity and selection, or keep identity only for a handful of three-to-nine-work lineages.

2. It is the only one whose titles, plot lengths and documentation were checked against the articles and not taken from memory. The scout's warning from that check applies to the others: 39 of 72 adaptation articles it probed turned out unusable.

3. Each outcome says something. If identity fails again against 160 detective films, "a canon is names plus genre" holds for two franchises. A selection null would mean something for the first time. Heredity can be split into straight, credited and "elements" pairs.

What it does not fix, and should not be sold as fixing: words still find half the sources, the names are kept so the placeholder codes return, and recognition will be high. It is a better-powered replication on a second franchise. For those three limits, add the remake arm described under what to take from the others.

What I checked myself:
- Live Wikipedia answered one small API request I sent from this machine to test the scout's claim. So the premise that it is unreachable was wrong, and the corpus can be fetched live, as the Batman corpus was.
- The scout's cache holds 201 article texts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-phylomemetics/a789a30b-498f-5fe1-bc57-f1de263eb0f6/scratchpad/corpus/franchise/raw/. I recomputed its word summary from /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-phylomemetics/a789a30b-498f-5fe1-bc57-f1de263eb0f6/scratchpad/corpus/franchise/pairs_result.json: the first-named source is ranked first for 16 of 32 and below tenth for 11. That matches.
- The local film table holds the Holmes films at the lengths stated. The negatives rule gives 159 films with my sentence splitter (the scout says 162), 92 of them from the 1930s and 1940s.

Not checked: no model was run, so every statement about recognition is an expectation.
first_author_aims.runner_up:
memorisation (Indian cross-industry remakes, with the East Asian contrast block).

It and "power" are the same corpus under different rules, and their scores tie. I prefer this version because its design does the one thing Holmes cannot: it sets a main set of mostly obscure films against a block the models should recognise, asks the recognition question first, and repeats every analysis on pairs where the model names neither film. Names differ without any edit, so there are no placeholder codes. Every plot is already in the local table.

It is second and not first because it is not a franchise. It has no canon, so there is no identity test in the paper's sense and no selection test. Words are also at ceiling on it, so it can only answer the "beyond words" question through the residual test.

If the first author wants a second franchise as a fallback, the Holmes scout's checked alternative is James Bond: all 26 films are in the local table and all 14 Fleming books have plot sections, but it yields only about 18 pairs and words rank the source first for 12 of them, so it would repeat Batman at twice the size.
first_author_aims.what_to_take_from_the_others:
**Run the remakes as a second, heredity-only arm beside Holmes.** This is the main thing. It covers the three limits Holmes leaves open (placeholder codes, recognition, low power for the residual test), needs no new plot text and costs minutes of GPU.

From "memorisation":
- Its rules: 15 sentences on both sides, different industries, pasted summaries (10% or more shared 5-word sequences) moved to a positive-control set, the rule fixed in advance and results reported both ways.
- The recognition question asked before anything else, and every analysis repeated on pairs the model does not name.
- The famous East Asian pairs as a contrast block, not as part of the main set.
- Retrieval among every film of the source's industry, where words are not at ceiling.
- Rebuild the pair list from the articles' leads, not from memory. With Wikipedia reachable this is about 150 small requests, not a 20 GB scan.
- Check each table row holds the right film's plot (it found wrong-article rows).

From "power":
- The longer list (105 pairs) as the starting point for that rebuild.
- The 2,977 background plots as extra decoy sources: their unit presence is already stored, so they cost nothing. This applies to Holmes too.
- The 24 loose Hollywood-to-Hindi pairs as a pre-declared secondary stratum where words are weak.
- Strip actors' names in brackets.

From "divergence", for the Holmes build:
- A second name-free version that swaps names for other ordinary names, not codes. It removes the placeholder mark that limited the Batman result.
- A link probe: ask each model which older work a text retells, not only which work it is.
- Cut sentences that name the source or its author.
- Relabel sources in the null so that adaptations of one source stay together (six works adapt The Hound).
- Never choose or drop pairs by their word-overlap rank.
- Faithful versions as a positive control that both words and units must pass.
- Its few zero-doubt transposed pairs (Seven Samurai to The Magnificent Seven and the like) are already inside the remake lists; the rest is not worth building now.
first_author_aims.doubts_about_the_winner:
1. **Recognition.** These are the most reproduced detective stories in English. If the 70B model names nearly every story, the heredity and identity results carry the same doubt as Batman's, and the split by recognition has nothing on one side. No model has been run to find out.

2. **The clean heredity set is small.** Tiers A and B are 19 adaptations on 12 distinct sources, and 6 of the 19 adapt The Hound. That is about twice Batman, not three and a half times. By my rough figure the standard error of the test statistic falls from about 0.10 (9 pairs) to 0.07 (19) or 0.05 (32); the remake sets reach 0.03. Thirteen of the 32 are episodes of one series, written and probably summarised by the same people.

3. **The pairs words miss are the weakly documented ones.** Tier C is "inspired by", "uses minor plot elements", "the title is inspired by". If neither words nor units find them, nothing is learned. So the question of whether units add to words will probably stay open on this corpus.

4. **The tiers were drawn in the same session as the word ranks.** They need to be re-derived from the articles' wording by a written rule, blind to the ranks, before the plan is frozen. The "first-named source" rule was also not applied consistently (see the pairs field).

5. **Placeholder codes return.** Holmes, Watson, Moriarty and Lestrade keep their names in every pair but Zero Effect.

6. **Identity has two confounds.** Period: Holmes screen works cluster in 1939 to 1946 and 2010 to 2017, and only 16 of the negatives are from the 2010s. Source of text: the negatives would come from a 2017 copy of Wikipedia while the Holmes texts are live 2026 articles. The negatives should be re-fetched live too. The 61 prose stories should stay out of the identity test, since every negative is a film.

7. **Selection can run backwards.** A story's pageviews are partly caused by its adaptations, and famous stories have longer plot sections. It needs controls for length and for how often a story is adapted.

8. **Live access is slow and may not last.** Requests took 6 to 30 seconds for the scout. The fetched texts should be saved with their revision numbers on the first pass.

9. **Overlap with the reference corpus.** Eleven Holmes films are in it and three are among the background plots that set base rates.
first_author_aims.pairs_you_believe_are_wrong:
I found no pair that I am confident is wrongly documented. These are the ones I would not count, or would check first.

**Holmes (replication)**
- The Sign of Three to The Sign of the Four: the article supports a title and one character name, not an adaptation.
- The Final Problem (Sherlock) to The Musgrave Ritual: one riddle song.
- The Great Game to The Bruce-Partington Plans: one named element.
- Terror by Night: its own article calls it "a mostly original story" with "minor plot elements". The scout's file also lists Lady Frances Carfax as its first source, where the quoted sentence names The Blue Carbuncle first.
- The Spider Woman: the first-named source (The Sign of the Four) is ranked 31st by words while The Final Problem, named in the same sentence, is ranked 1st. The "first-named" rule is arbitrary for films with several sources.
- "The Story of the Lost Special": I believe the article's title is "The Lost Special". Check the resolved title.

**Remakes (power and memorisation)**
