- Enakkul Oruvan (1984) to Karz and Samrat (1997) to Baazigar: I believe both are right, and the table rows look like the right films, but words rank the source 1,153rd and 785th, so read both plots in full before keeping them.

**Retellings (divergence)**
- Frozen to The Snow Queen and The Princess and the Frog to The Frog Prince: documented, but almost nothing of the source's plot survives, so they test nothing.
- Warm Bodies, The Bad Sleep Well, Jubal and Forbidden Planet: the link is made by critics or by the novel's article, as the scout says.
- Hard Target: the article bases it on the 1932 film, so the source should be that film and not the short story.
- You've Got Mail: the documented source is the play Parfumerie, by way of the 1940 film.

scores.comment:
Sherlock Holmes. It is the only franchise among the four and the only proposal whose documentation was read from the live articles. I checked six of its quotations against its cached article text and its sixteen film rows against the local table, and all hold. Its pool of wrong candidates is the fairest of the four: 60 stories by one author about one detective, all older than every adaptation.

The pair count shrinks under discount. Of the 33 adaptations, 13 are tier C ("inspired by", "uses minor plot elements", "the title is inspired by") and should not count as documented descent. That leaves 20 (7 straight, 12 credited or loosely based, 1 pastiche) resting on 13 distinct sources. Six of the 20 are The Hound of the Baskervilles, and three of the credited films take a single device from the story. The effective sample is about 13 to 17, against Batman's 9 adaptations on 7 sources. By my approximation the smallest shift the rank test can detect falls from about 0.24 to about 0.18 of the candidates beating the source, so the test of neurons against words stays underpowered.

Confounds: 13 adaptations are consecutive episodes of one television series with the same three writers and running story arcs; the Universal films share cast, director and the years 1942 to 1946. Words rank the source first for all 7 straight adaptations and for half overall, and the pairs words miss are the weakly documented ones, where there may be no trail for anything to find. Names are shared, so the placeholder codes return. Recognition will be at least as high as for Batman.

What it does buy is the two experiments no other proposal supports. Identity gets rule-chosen negatives (I reproduced the rule and got 156, not 162). But 91 of them are from the 1930s and 1940s, only 16 from the 2010s, and none is television, so the 13 Sherlock episodes have almost no negatives matched for period or medium. Selection gets 60 early works; I confirm about 75% power against a correlation of 0.3, where Batman had 27%.

Cross-language remakes, 105 pairs on 92 sources. "Remake of" in the remake's own lead is the strongest documentation of descent in any proposal. It rested on memory, so I tested it: I drew 40 pairs at random from this list and the memorisation list together and read the remakes' leads on live Wikipedia. 39 of 40 state the claimed source (34 of 34 from this list). 82 of the 92 sources have a single remake, so the pairs are close to independent, and the smallest detectable shift is about 0.07 to 0.08, a third of Batman's. Names differ without any editing. Every plot is in the local table, and the decoys' unit presence is already stored for all four models (I checked the files exist).

Its weakness is that words solve the heredity test outright. My own check on the 105: the median TF-IDF cosine to the true source is 0.20 against 0.05 to the other sources; the source is ranked first for 84% of remakes (91% within its own industry); 0.9% of other sources beat it; and only 0.04% of wrong-candidate cells reach the median similarity of a true pair. The paper's residual regression would therefore be extrapolating: there are almost no wrong candidates as word-similar as the right one. The test has to be recast against hard negatives from the large pool, where words leave 27 to 44 pairs unsolved.

Other points against: the primary set mixes 19 famous East Asian and Hollywood pairs with the Indian ones; 20 of the 105 have a plot of only 10 to 14 sentences; at least 12 pairs are the director's own remake and actors recur; the pool across nine film industries is only fair if it is stratified by industry and period, as the proposal plans. There is no identity or selection test, and it is not a franchise.

Transposed retellings, 80 pairs on 48 sources. The proposal is honest about its own pilot: words do as well here as on Batman (11.7% of wrong sources beat the true one, against 11%), and the source is first for 28 of 59. It is still the best of the four on this criterion, with a Shakespeare block where words are weaker (17%). But the pilot stood in a faithful film for each play or novel, so the real source texts were never measured.

Under discount I count about 36 to 39 flat credits or stated adaptations. The other half are "loosely based on", "inspired by" or critics' readings, and several carry little plot (Frozen, The Princess and the Frog, The Lion King, Easy A). The live leads I read confirm the softness: Jubal "has been described as an Othello on the Range", Forbidden Planet is one that "many consider" a loose adaptation, and the leads of Ball of Fire and Warm Bodies name no source at all.

The pool is the least fair. It mixes plays, novels, fairy tales, epics and films, whose Wikipedia synopses differ in register and length, and the 24 decoy sources were picked by hand. A film-to-film pair has only about a dozen same-medium candidates.

The worst confound runs in the direction that produces a false pass. These are famous films with their names left in, and the link itself is common knowledge (Clueless is Emma). A unit could fire for the source because the model recalls the fact. The proposal's link probe is the right guard, but nobody knows how many pairs would survive it. Feasibility is moderate: about 100 articles still have to be fetched, three sources may have no usable plot text, and sentences that name the source have to be cut by hand.

Indian cross-industry remakes, 78 pairs on 70 sources. This is the same corpus as the power proposal with a tighter design: 59 of its 78 pairs are in both lists. Under equal rules (both plots of 15 sentences or more, Indian films only) it actually holds more pairs than the power list, 78 against about 62.

It has the better statistical discipline. The primary set is homogeneous. The wrong candidates are near neighbours chosen by rule (same industry, within five years, a median of 288 per remake). The pair list is to be rebuilt mechanically from the articles' leads, which removes the bias of a list recalled from memory. Each table row is to be checked against its article, because the table links some rows to the wrong film. The famous East Asian pairs are kept apart as a block the models should recognise. Recognition is asked first, including which film a plot remakes.

In my random sample 21 of its 22 pairs were confirmed by the live lead, and the three it marked "fairly sure" (Samrat, Bharathan, Khuddar) are all confirmed. One pair breaks its own rule (Kushi, see below).

The word problem is the same as for power, and the proposal says so: words find these sources more easily than Batman's (62 of 78 first among the 70 sources). The claim of low memorisation is plausible but unmeasured. Names stay in the text, many titles are the hero's name, and 90 of the 147 films are in the project's own reference corpus. Scoring the hard-negative pool needs one extra GPU pass on about 3,600 plots, which is cheap. There is no identity or selection test, and it is not a franchise.

statistician.recommendation:
Choose the cross-language remake corpus: the power proposal's list and extra blocks, built by the memorisation proposal's rules. They are one corpus, and I name power as the winner only because it is the superset.

This departs from the first author's own word, which was "franchise". The reason is the pair count. No franchise delivers it: Holmes, checked live, gives about 20 firmly documented adaptations on 13 sources, roughly twice Batman, and the test of neurons against words would again end as an absence of evidence. If a franchise is a requirement and not a preference, take Holmes and accept that limit.

Why the remakes win on the points I was asked to weigh:

1. **Documented pairs.** About 100 pairs on about 90 sources, each stated as a remake in the remake's own lead. My random live check confirmed 39 of 40. That is a five-fold gain in independent pairs, and it is the only proposal in which a null on the residual test would be a bounded negative.
2. **Names.** They differ by the nature of the adaptation, so the original texts can be tested and the placeholder codes are no longer the only condition.
3. **Recognition.** Most of the films are regional releases, with a famous block alongside, so the result can be split by whether the model names the films. With 9 pairs that split was impossible.
4. **Cost.** Every plot is in the local table and the decoys' unit presence is already stored.

What it cannot show: identity and selection, in the paper's sense. And the heredity test itself will be trivially passed by words and units alike; all the information is in whether units add to words.

Three conditions I would attach before any model reads a text:

- **Recast the decision test.** True pairs sit far outside the wrong pairs in word similarity (0.20 against 0.05), so a regression fitted on wrong pairs extrapolates. Test the units against each remake's nearest candidates by words, drawn from several thousand films of the same industry and period, for example with a conditional logit that has the word measures as covariates. Then put word-only measures and a sentence embedding through the same test in the units' place, as the paper did, to show it cannot be passed without units.
- **Make the primary set homogeneous.** Indian cross-industry pairs with both plots at 15 sentences or more, the list rebuilt from the leads and not from memory, relabelling within industry and period, and families of one source kept together.
- **Verify the documentation live.** Live Wikipedia does answer from this machine, though it is rate-limited (two of my five requests were refused). Twenty leads come back per request, so the whole list can be checked and quoted in about seven requests, with no need for the 20 GB dump.
statistician.runner_up:
Replication (Sherlock Holmes).

By score the memorisation proposal ties with the winner, but it is the same corpus and should be merged into it, not run as an alternative. The real alternative is Holmes. It is the only proposal that keeps all three experiments, it is a franchise as the first author asked, and its work list is already verified against the live articles.

It also complements the remakes exactly. It supplies the identity test (about 156 rule-chosen negatives against 8) and the selection test (60 early works, about 75% power against 27%), which the remakes cannot. Running the models is cheap and its list is built, so it could follow as a second arm. If it does, its primary set should be the 20 adaptations of tiers A and B, with the six Hound works averaged, and its negatives matched by decade.
statistician.what_to_take_from_the_others:
**From memorisation (into the winner)**
- Rebuild the pair list mechanically from the remakes' leads; treat the recalled lists as a check on recall.
- Primary set: Indian cross-industry pairs, both plots at 15 sentences or more.
- Wrong candidates: films of the same industry within five years, outside the remake's family.
- Compare each table row's plot with its article, because some rows hold another film's plot. Remove verbatim duplicates (57 Indian plots appear under two titles).
- Ask recognition first, including "which film does this remake?".
- Leave the study films out of the unit scales and base rates: 90 of the 147 are in the reference corpus.
- Keep the East Asian pairs as a separate block the models should recognise.

**From replication (Holmes)**
- The finding that live Wikipedia is reachable, and its method: quote and store the documenting sentence for every pair, and reject any title that resolves to its source's article.
- Tiers by the wording of the documentation, with the primary tier fixed in advance.
- A title-only control. The remake table has natural ones: unrelated films that share a title.
- Averaging within a source that has several adaptations.
- Holmes itself as the later franchise arm for identity and selection.

**From divergence**
- The link probe, and reporting every result separately for pairs where the model does and does not name the link.
- A sensitivity version with the names swapped for other ordinary names, not codes.
- Cutting sentences that name the source ("This movie is a remake of ..."), and adding the count of shared names to the measures regressed out.
- The rule never to choose or drop pairs by their word-overlap rank, which would manufacture a win for units.
- Faithful and partly renamed versions as positive controls.
- Its nine film-to-film genre-shift pairs, which are complete in the local table, and a small pre-registered loose block as the place where words are weak.

**From power's own secondary sets**
- The copied pairs as a positive control.
- The 24 loose pairs as a registered secondary stratum. Two of them (Samrat from Baazigar, Bharathan from Ghayal) are stated as remakes in the live leads and can move to the firm set.
statistician.doubts_about_the_winner:
1. **Words nearly separate true pairs from wrong ones, so the planned residual test is not identified.** On the 105 pairs the source is ranked first by TF-IDF for 84%, and almost no wrong candidate is as word-similar as the right one. A linear regression on word measures would be extrapolating, and a measure that is merely a curved function of word overlap could pass in the units' place. The test must be recast against hard negatives and calibrated with word-only measures. Even then the information comes from the 27 to 44 pairs that words leave unsolved, and some of those will be table errors, not hard cases.
2. **Edited copying.** The screen removes verbatim copies (10% of 5-word sequences). A summary pasted from the source's article and then reworded keeps its sentence order, which units could detect and word counts would not. A pass would then show text reuse, not story inheritance. Report the result against the degree of copying, and on the pairs with none.
3. **Hidden relatives in the wrong-candidate pool.** Other remakes of the same source, and the source's own source, sit among the "wrong" films. The memorisation scout found about 96 close pairs nobody had listed. Unless they are removed they count against both words and units.
4. **Simultaneous productions.** One of my 40 sampled pairs, Kushi (2001), is described in its lead as planned as a bilingual with the Tamil film, by the same director, and is not called a remake. Kuselan and Kathanayakudu are one production in two languages, both listed as remakes of one source. Same-year pairs (Gemini, Naa Autograph, Minnale and its Hindi version, Veede) need the same reading.
5. **Shared makers.** At least 12 pairs are the director's own remake, and actors recur. Cast names in brackets must be stripped.
6. **Recognition is unmeasured.** Names stay in the text and many titles are the hero's name, so naming a film is easier than on Batman's name-free texts. The lead states the remake link, so a model may know it. If the 70B model names most of these films, the main reason for the Indian set goes.
7. **A list recalled from memory leans towards better-known films.** Rebuilding it from the leads fixes this, but the size of the final set is then unknown.
8. **It is a new statistic.** Batman's inheritance rate is scored against the lineage's own non-adapting works. Remake families have no such baseline, so the numbers will not be comparable with the paper's 15% against 46%, and the new design needs its own frozen plan.
9. **A pass would still be modest.** Two editors describing one plot use different words for the same events, so any measure of meaning should beat word counts. Without an embedding comparator, "units add to words" could be over-read.
10. **It is not what the first author named.** Identity and selection are left untested, and the paper would still rest on one franchise for both.

**What I did and did not check.** I read the paper sections, the local table and the scouts' scratch files. I made five small requests to the Wikipedia API (two were refused for rate), covering the leads of 60 articles. I ran no model and opened no dump. Nothing in the repository was written and git was not run. My scratch files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-phylomemetics/a789a30b-498f-5fe1-bc57-f1de263eb0f6/scratchpad/corpus/judge-statistician/. The power figures are my own normal approximations, treating each adaptation's rank as uniform under the null.
statistician.pairs_you_believe_are_wrong:
**Power and memorisation (remakes)**

Checked: 40 pairs drawn at random from the two lists together, plus 10 I doubted, read in the remakes' live leads.
- Wrong under the proposals' own rule: **Kushi (2001, Telugu) from Kushi (2000, Tamil)**, in the memorisation list. The lead says it was planned as a bilingual with the Tamil film, by the same director, and does not call it a remake.
- Dependent, not wrong: Kuselan and Kathanayakudu (one production in two languages, both from Katha Parayumbol); The Ring and Ring (both adapt one novel); Wanted (its lead says remake of the Telugu Pokiri, but its director had made the Tamil version).
- Table error: Okkadu is labelled Malayalam with the wrong year in the power list's file.
- Confirmed against my doubt: Samrat, Bharathan, Khuddar, 20 Once Again, Jeena Sirf Merre Liye, Aegan, Tubelight ("an adaptation of").
- From memory I believe the remaining pairs are right. I found none I think is wrong.

**Replication (Holmes)**

The quotations are real. The discount is for looseness.
- Do not count tier C (13 adaptations). The weakest: The Sign of Three (title only); The Final Problem (Sherlock) to The Musgrave Ritual (a reference); Terror by Night ("minor plot elements" of four stories); The Blind Banker (the idea of coded messages); The Great Game (one of several cases); The Abominable Bride; The Spider Woman, where the first-named source is ranked 31st by words and another named source is ranked first, so the choice of source decides the result.
- Tier B in name only: Sherlock Holmes and the Secret Weapon (its article says the code is the only element taken); Sherlock Holmes and the Voice of Terror; The House of Fear.
- Out of the pool: The Reichenbach Fall to The Woman in Green (film to film); The Empty Hearse to The Lost Special.
- My count of firm pairs: 20 adaptations on 13 sources, of which about 17 carry real plot. Four tier C pairs do carry plot and could be a registered secondary set: The Reichenbach Fall, The Empty Hearse, A Game of Shadows, Dressed to Kill.

**Divergence (retellings)**

- Critics' readings, not documentation: Jubal, Forbidden Planet, Warm Bodies (film), Ball of Fire (nothing in the lead). The Bad Sleep Well is better than feared: its lead says it "draws upon" Hamlet.
- Little or no plot carried: Frozen, The Princess and the Frog, The Lion King, The Lion King II, Easy A, Strange Brew, O Brother Where Art Thou?, Bridget Jones's Diary.
- More than one source: Assault on Precinct 13 (its lead names two inspirations), Phantom of the Paradise, Ran.
- Wrong direct parent: Hard Target (its lead says the 1932 film); Man Pasand (its lead says My Fair Lady and a Marathi play).
- No single source text: the two Faust films, The Warriors (Anabasis), and the fairy tales, whose articles summarise several variants.
- My count of flat credits or stated adaptations: about 36 to 39 of the 80.
